pages.name: Two at right angles
pages.task: Two voltages in series are 6 V at 0° and 8 V at 90°. What is their total size?
pages.why: √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 V. The drops inside a transformer add the same way.

pages.name: Loading
pages.text: Off load the output reaches the 115 V circle. On load, two drops sit tip to tail on the output arrow. One is across the windings' resistance, the other across their reactance. The last tip stays on the circle, so the output shortens.

pages.name: Full load, unity
pages.task: At full load and unity power factor, the drop is 4.6 V in line with the output and 3.45 V across it. The arrows close on 115 V. What is the output, to two decimal places?
pages.why: √(115² − 3.45²) = 114.95 V along the axis. The 3.45 V across costs only 0.05 V. Take off the 4.6 V: 110.35 V.

pages.text: At 0.8 lagging the drop lines up with the output. The whole 5.75 V comes off, leaving 109.25 V. Regulation is the sag as a share of the no-load voltage: 5.0%.

pages.name: Regulation at unity
pages.task: At unity power factor the output is 110.35 V against 115 V at no load. What is the regulation?
pages.why: 4.65 ÷ 115 = 0.040, so 4.0%. It is less than at 0.8 lagging. Here the 3.45 V points across the output.

pages.name: Predict: leading
pages.task: Before you see it, predict. At full load, will 0.8 leading sag more or less than unity?
pages.why: A leading current swings the drop forward, away from the output. Less of the drop then lies along the output. So the output sags less than at unity.

pages.name: Leading
pages.text: With a leading load, less of the drop lies along the output, so the output rises. It is 113.26 V at 0.8 leading. Past 0.6 leading the drop points back. At 0.5 leading the output is 115.55 V, above no load.

pages.name: Above no load
pages.task: At 0.5 leading the output is 115.55 V against 115 V at no load. What is the regulation?
pages.why: −0.55 ÷ 115 = −0.0048, so −0.5%. Negative regulation means the output rose on load.

pages.name: A quick rule
pages.text: Regulation ≈ R% cos φ + X% sin φ, the parts of the two drops along the output. Take sin φ as negative when leading. R% is the full-load copper loss as a share of the rating. With R% at 4 and X% at 3, that gives 5.0% at 0.8 lagging and 1.4% at 0.8 leading.

pages.name: Another transformer
pages.task: A transformer has an R% of 1.5 and an X% of 3. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 lagging?

pages.name: Percentage impedance
pages.text: Percentage impedance is the share of rated voltage that drives rated current through a short. Here it is 5%. So with a stiff supply, full voltage drives 20 times rated current, 1739 A. A lower impedance gives less drop and more fault current.

pages.name: A 4% unit
pages.task: A 20 kVA, 115 V transformer has 4% impedance. What current flows into a dead short at its terminals?
pages.why: 20,000 ÷ 115 = 173.91 A rated. 100 ÷ 4 = 25, and 173.91 × 25 = 4348 A. Twice the rating at the same impedance gives twice the fault current.

pages.name: Leading, another unit
pages.task: A transformer has an R% of 2 and an X% of 4. What is its regulation at full load, 0.8 leading?
pages.why: 1.6 − 2.4 = −0.8%. The output rises a little above no load.

pages.name: Choosing an impedance
pages.task: A board needs a small volt drop and a low fault current. You can fit a 4% or an 8% transformer of the same rating. Which is true of the two?
pages.answer: 4% gives less drop, 8% less fault current
pages.why: The 8% unit's drop is about twice the 4% unit's. Its fault current is about half. One impedance cannot make both small. So you choose by which limit is tighter.
options: 8% gives less drop and less fault current
4% gives less drop and less fault current
4% gives less drop, 8% less fault current
8% gives less drop, 4% less fault current
